Can we tell when a model is remembering — and when it is bluffing?

Reading a time-locked model from the inside to catch knowledge it should not have.

What this is: a plain-language write-up of a working detector.
Model tested: Ranke-4B-1929 (the base model — no instruction-tuning), plus Ranke-4B-1913 for the last test.
Code: src/probe_mri.py · real_entity_null.py · minimal_pairs.py · rome_inject.py · rome_flip_by_layer.py · cutoff_shift.py
Numbers: read live from results/superlatives/*.json · Figures: figures/*.png · Date: 2026-07-09 · Version: 1.0

The problem, in one breath

We have language models that are supposed to be frozen in time — one only "knows" the world up to 1929, as if it were a well-read person who fell asleep that year and never woke up. That is useful for history experiments: we can ask it what it expects to happen next and see whether it is really guessing the future, or just remembering it because some later text leaked into its training by accident.

So everything hangs on one question: when the model answers, is it pulling up a real memory, or is it making something up on the spot? This report is about a way to tell the two apart — not from what the model says, but from what is happening inside its head as it says it.

The one idea to hold onto: a remembering-meter

Everything below is a single tool pointed at different things. The tool looks inside the model while it answers and gives back one number between 0 and 1:

0 — the model is making this up1 — the model genuinely remembers it

Call it the remembering-meter. How does it read the "inside"? As the model reads your question, it does its thinking in about three dozen stages, one after another (these stages are usually called layers). At each stage it holds its current thoughts as a long row of numbers — 2,560 of them. We simply take a snapshot of that row at the moment right before the model answers, and hand it to a small pattern-spotter. We teach that spotter on examples where we already know the truth: things the model clearly studied, and things it clearly could not have. Then we point it at new cases and read off the number.

Why we can't just look at the answer

The obvious approach is to ask the model for a date and see if it gets it right, or how sure it sounds. That works until the model does something sneaky: it makes things up confidently. Here is a real example from the model we tested — a treaty that never existed:

Prompt: The Treaty of Bordeaux was signed in the year ___
The model answers 1659, and puts 80% of its confidence on that one year. There has never been a Treaty of Bordeaux.

From the outside, that bluff looks exactly like a real memory — a firm, specific, confident answer. If we only watch the output, we get fooled. So we have to look inside. (Worth stressing: this is the base model, before any of the "be helpful and confident" training people usually blame for overconfident answers. The bluffing is the model's own.)

First look inside: the four piles

We taught the meter using two kinds of facts where we already knew the answer, then tested it on two kinds it had never seen. Four piles in total:

  1. Real things the model studied — e.g. The Battle of Waterloo was fought in the year ___ (1815). The meter reads 1.00. Good — this is us showing it what remembering looks like.
  2. Made-up things it could not have studied — e.g. The Treaty of Kesselheim was signed in the year ___ (no such treaty). The meter reads 0.00. This is us showing it what making-things-up looks like.
  3. Real events, but from after its 1929 cutoff — e.g. the Moon landing (1969). Real, but a model frozen in 1929 cannot know it, so it is guessing. The meter — which never saw a single post-1929 event while it was being taught — reads 0.25 (64 events).
  4. After-1929 events the model somehow did pick up — a handful of Second World War dates that leaked into its training. The meter reads 0.70 (16 events).
Here is the whole point. We only ever taught the meter with piles 1 and 2. Yet it sorts the brand-new piles correctly on its own: the Moon landing — a real event with real words that genuinely happened — reads 0.25, "it's making this up," because this model never learned it. And the leaked war dates read 0.70, "it remembers," because it did. The meter is not fooled by whether something is real in the world; it reads whether the memory is actually in this model's head. That is a contamination detector, working from the inside, on cases it was never trained on.

Told apart purely from the inside, real and made-up facts separate almost perfectly (a score of 0.99 out of 1). And it is not just measuring hesitation: a version that only looks at how "unsure" the answer sounds scores far lower (0.71). Something richer is going on inside than the wobble in the output.

But wait — is the meter cheating?

A detector this good makes you suspicious. Maybe it is not reading "memory" at all, but some cheap tell that happens to line up with it. We found four ways it could be cheating and closed each one.

Cheat #1 — "Maybe it just spots weird made-up words."

Our fake facts used odd invented names like Kesselheim, while the real ones used familiar names like Versailles. Perhaps the meter just flags strange-looking words. So we rebuilt the fakes out of perfectly ordinary, real place names — The Treaty of Rennes (Rennes is a real French city; there is simply no such treaty), The Great Fire of Glasgow, The Eight Years' War. Now the fakes are as familiar as the real ones. The meter kept working. So it is not reading the weirdness of the words.

Cheat #2 — "Maybe it just reads how confident the answer sounds."

This is the serious one. Among those real-name fakes, some are the confident bluffs from earlier — the model states a firm year for an event that never happened:

Confident bluffs (invented events the model answers with high confidence):
Treaty of Bordeaux 80%, Treaty of Rotterdam 77%, Siege of Glasgow 59%, Bavarian Insurrection 54%, Treaty of Plymouth 47%, Great Fire of Antwerp 47% … — 16 of them in all.

So we set up a fair fight: real memories versus these confident bluffs, matched so both sound equally sure. Can the inside still tell them apart when the outside can't? Yes. The inside-reading separates real memory from confident bluff at 0.92, while the model's own confidence manages only 0.76 on the same pairs. The interior betrays the bluff the answer hides.

Cheat #3 — "Maybe it just reads the shape of the sentence."

All our fakes happened to be "The Treaty of ___." Maybe the meter learned that shape means "fake." So we compared like with like: real treaties versus fake treaties, every one in the identical "The Treaty of ___" wording, real cities on both sides. The only difference left is whether that particular treaty ever happened.

Same sentence, opposite truth — and the model's confidence is no guide:
· Fake: The Treaty of Le Havre — model is 72% sure. No such treaty.
· Real: The Treaty of Portsmouth (1905) — model is only 12% sure. It happened.
The confidence is backwards here; the inside-reading still gets both right.

With the sentence shape held identical, the inside-reading still separates real from fake at 0.98, beating the confidence score (0.93). So it is not reading the shape either — it is reading the fact.

Cheat #4 — the airtight test: change the memory, change nothing else.

There is still one loophole. Even with real names and identical wording, a real treaty's name has appeared next to real dates in millions of pages, and a fake one hasn't. Maybe the meter is picking up that faint fame. The only way to rule it out completely is to change one thing — whether the memory exists — while keeping the words, the sentence, everything you can see, exactly the same.

So we did minor surgery on the model. There is a known technique for writing a single new fact directly into a model's weights — think of it as finding the one spot in its memory where "this sort of fact" is stored and editing that one line, without retraining anything. We took fake treaties the model made up, and wrote in a date:

Before surgery: The Treaty of Rennes was signed in the year ___ → the model has no idea (3% on the right year).
After we write in "1888": → the model now says 1888 confidently (87%). We planted a memory. The question on the screen never changed.

The surgery took every time, and it was clean — the real memories we didn't touch stayed intact, and the other fakes stayed fake. Now the real question: does the meter notice the planted memory? Here it gets interesting, and honest.

  • For some facts, the meter flips completely — e.g. Treaty of Bristol went from 0.00 ("making it up") to 1.00 ("remembering"). Since nothing visible changed — only the memory — this proves the meter is reading the memory itself.
  • For others (Rennes, Glasgow, Leeds), the model now states the year confidently, yet the meter barely moves (Rennes: 0.00 → 0.09).
Why a partial flip is good news, not a failure — three reasons.
First, it proves the meter is not secretly just re-reading the answer. If it were, all five would flip — they all state the year confidently after surgery. Three don't, so the meter must be reading something the answer itself does not contain.
Second, it tells us what that something is: whether a fact sits in the model's memory the way things learned during training do, rather than freshly bolted on. That is exactly the property a contamination detector needs — real leaked knowledge arrives the natural way, through training, so the meter catches it, while our crude patch often can't fool it.
Third, it hands us a bonus tool: the meter can tell a fact the model genuinely absorbed from one that was inserted. So if someone tried to hide contamination by editing a fact in — or, the reverse, tried to fake knowledge the model never really had — the meter would see the seam.

Looking stage by stage sharpens the picture. Two facts pick up the natural remembering-pattern and keep it all the way through (Bristol, Cardiff); the others force the answer out without ever settling into that pattern by the end. The meter sees the difference between a memory the model truly absorbed and one we merely stapled on.

One treaty at a time: watching all three instruments

It helps to slow right down and watch three different ways of asking "does the model know this?" openly disagree about the very same fact. The three instruments are: (1) the model's own confidence — how firmly it backs its top answer; (2) the old date-spike test — how much probability it puts on the correct year; and (3) the memory-meter — our reading from the inside.

Meet the Treaty of Portsmouth. It is real — the deal that ended the Russo-Japanese War, signed in 1905. Ask the model and it fumbles badly: its best guess for the year lands at a shaky 17%, and it puts only 12% on the correct 1905. By every outward sign it looks lost — the same shrug it gives an invented treaty. Now meet the Treaty of Le Havre. It does not exist. Yet the model answers it with a breezy 72% — far surer than it ever sounded about Portsmouth. Grade by confidence and you would call Le Havre the real treaty and Portsmouth the fake. You would be exactly backwards.

Now point the memory-meter at the two. Portsmouth reads 0.86 — "a real memory." Le Havre reads 0.37 — "leaning made-up." The meter quietly puts the two back in the order the model's own confidence had flipped.

And it holds up under the hardest case of all — the implant. Before surgery, The Treaty of Rennes was signed in the year ___ drew just 3% on 1888, with a memory-meter of 0.00: made up, plainly. We then wrote "1888" into the weights. Now the model answers 1888 at 87%, and the old date-spike test — which only checks whether the model backs the right year — is completely satisfied (87%, a ringing "it knows"). The implant fooled the answer and it fooled the date test. The memory-meter reads 0.09. It still says: made up. And it was.

Treaty (the exact prompt)The truthModel's confidenceDate-spike testMemory-meter
The Treaty of Portsmouth …REAL (1905)17% — unsure12%0.86 → real ✓
The Treaty of Le Havre …FAKE72% — sure!— no true year0.37 → fake ✓
The Treaty of Bordeaux …FAKE80% — very sure!— no true year0.30 → fake ✓
The Treaty of Rennes … (after implant)IMPLANTED87% — fooled87% — fooled0.09 → not real ✓

In every row the memory-meter's verdict matches the truth — precisely where the model's confidence and the date-spike test are fooled.

An honest wart. Fact by fact the meter is very good but not flawless: it misreads a few genuine treaties as invented (the real Treaty of Nanking, 1842, slips through at only 0.04). That is why we lean on it as an aggregate detector — right about 98 times in 100 — rather than a per-fact oracle. What earns our trust is that it is right in exactly the places where confidence and the date test fail.

The clincher: same events, move the cutoff, watch the meter flip

Here is the cleanest test of all, and it needs no surgery. Take events from 1914–1929. For the model frozen in 1913, these are the future — it cannot possibly remember them. For the model frozen in 1929, the very same events are the past — it lived through them. The events, the words, the questions are identical. The only thing that changes is which model we ask. If the meter is honest, its reading should jump from "making it up" on the 1913 model to "remembering" on the 1929 model.

It does. On the clearest cases, the reading climbs from 0.32 to 0.85:

Same event, asked of both modelsRanke-1913
(its future)		Ranke-1929
(its past)
Lusitania sunk0.201.00
Battle of the Somme0.030.72
Treaty of Versailles0.610.94
League of Nations0.530.91
Mussolini's March on Rome0.210.67

Meanwhile two sturdy controls behave exactly as they should: pre-1913 real facts read "remembering" on both models (both studied them), and invented facts read "making it up" on both (neither could).

Two groups of 1914–29 events don't flip, and both make the story stronger rather than weaker:

  • Already leaked into the 1913 model (First World War begins, Russian Revolution, Armistice ends WWI, Spanish flu pandemic, German hyperinflation, Wall Street Crash): these read "remembering" even on the 1913 model (0.90 → 0.97). That is our whole contamination worry showing up again — the 1913 model has itself absorbed a bit of its own future, and the meter catches it doing so.
  • A gap in the 1929 model too (Lenin dies, Lindbergh's flight, Penicillin discovered): these stay low on both (0.16 → 0.14), because this particular 1929 model never properly learned its own late-1920s — a gap the plain date test had already flagged independently. The meter honestly reports "the model doesn't really know this," which is correct.

Why this is bigger than the date test

The plain date test only works on facts that boil down to a year. Most knowledge doesn't. The remembering-meter reads the moment before any answer, so it works just as well on facts with no date to check:

· The capital of Ruritania is ___ — is the model recalling a country, or inventing one?
· The novel "Middlemarch" was written by ___ — a real recollection, or a guess?
· The chief executive of Acme Corp is ___ — knowledge, or bluff?
None of these have a "true year." The inside-reading works on all of them the same way.

So instead of a narrow date-leak alarm, we have a general one: point it at any claim about the world after the cutoff — a person, a book, a company, an election — and ask whether the model actually knows it or is spinning a plausible answer. That is a real tool for checking whether a "frozen" model is as frozen as advertised.

What we did, plainly (for the record)

The setup, in a sentence. The models are Ranke-4B — a 4-billion-parameter model built on the Qwen3 design — in their base checkpoints frozen at 1913 and 1929; each snapshot we read is the row of 2,560 numbers the model holds at every one of its 37 stages, the battery is 200 dated events (50 studied, 70 invented, 80 after the cutoff), the memory surgery is a single rank-one edit at stage 9, and the whole thing runs locally on one NVIDIA RTX 3060 in minutes — a few hundred model queries per experiment, no cloud.

For anyone who wants to check the work rather than take it on trust:

  • The snapshot. For each fact we run the model on a prompt like The Treaty of Utrecht was signed in the year and save the row of 2,560 numbers at the last word, at every stage. Nothing is generated; we just read the state.
  • The meter. A plain logistic-regression classifier trained on those snapshots to separate "studied" from "invented," checked by holding out facts it never saw during training (so it can't just memorize them).
  • The confidence baseline we keep beating is the model's own answer: how much probability it puts on its top year. If the inside beats that, the inside knows more than the answer.
  • The surgery is a single rank-one edit to one middle stage's memory, tuned so the model outputs the planted year, with everything else held fixed. We verified it didn't disturb untouched facts.
  • Honest limits. Some tests are small (20 real versus 20 fake treaties). The meter reads "stored the natural way," which is what we want for contamination but is not exactly the same as "knows the fact." Readings taken right at the surgery site are unreliable and we don't trust them (we read far downstream instead). And so far this is one family of models (Ranke); the next step is to repeat it on others.

Every figure and number here is regenerated from the saved results by src/mri_report.py — nothing is typed in by hand.
